messages.subject: Strange error on random effects model
messages.subject_clean: Strange error on random effects model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to fit a random effects model.

Have students who have taken repeated tests.  Want to fit both an intercept and slope to each student.  (Perhaps an AR1 on the slope?)

When running the model below, I get an error of:
"Error in if (nrep > 1 || ngroup > 1) { :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed"

There is no missing data in my dataframe, and no NA values.

Any suggestions on how to resolve this?

Thank You!

The model is:
(Note:  student2 is just a direct copy of student)

m <- inla(
score ~ 1
+ f(student, model = "iid")
+ f(student2, replicate=student, model = "ar1", values = 1:134, hyper=hyper1)
, data = df, family = "gaussian"
, control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, po=TRUE, config=TRUE)
, control.inla = list(strategy="auto", int.strategy="eb")
, verbose=T
)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] ar1c with replicate /group / etc
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for doing this :)

Does this mean INLA

(as standard)  cannot handle hierarchies like the one I outlined?

For the specific potential work-around, I'm not sure if this workaround would work for the application we have in mind. We are mostly interested in how covariates affect the change at each timestep, and we would be looking to have the covariate induced growth decay over time if the covariate effect is taken away (aka, including the AR rho parameter), so it would be useful to have these covariates internal to the AR process.

If it ends up being too complex to have internal to the AR, how would the "AR with trend" work when the covariates aren't all fixed to be 1 as in this toy example?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Average temporal trend
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom Johnson,

If your linear predictor is
  intercept + beta * covariate + spatio.temporal
as you mentioned, the spatio-temporal model term could capture the
temporal overall trend, but it needs to be summarized integrating over
space for each time.

However, you may want to add a term in the linear predictor to capture
it, particularly if there is an overall common trend. If you then have
  intercept + beta * covariate + temporal + spatio.temporal
then the temporal term will capture it.

Best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Excursion Estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am interested in studying spatial variation over a domain. As a part of this, I generate predictions on a fine grid and use the posterior samples from inla.posterior.sample to summarize the values of the spatial random effects.

I would like to generate excursion sets, and since I already have the posterior samples from inla.posterior.sample, I've been using the excursions.mc <http://excursions.mc> and continuous functions together. I am also aware of the excursions.inla function that could be used as well ... but when I use this function to compute the excursion sets, I get different results.

My model uses a Poisson likelihood (fairly low counts) and I am using the NIQC scheme for computing the excursions. Are there settings in INLA itself that might generate these differences? Do some of the newer settings that were recently introduced need to be adjusted? (IE: Simplified Laplace, VB Correction, Experimental Mode?)

I checked if the means and variances that are computed line up, and in general they do. Refer to first page of the attachments.

I then computed the differences of the summary from INLA against the marginal estimates from the posterior samples and the excursions functions. In this case, there appears to be a systematic skew for the excursion estimates. Second page of attachments.

Finally, treating each element as a Gaussian, I computed a z-score for each element to summarize the differences in mean and sd estimates between the outputs. Again, there appears to be a skew in the differences between the INLA summary and the excursion estimates.  Third page of attachments.

I also checked that increasing the number of samples decreases the errors for the MC method ... which result is more reliable?

messages.subject: Re: Excursion Estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I think that the difference might be caused by the VB corrections that are now used for the marginals in INLA, which therefore also would be used by excursions.inla.

If you instead sample from the posterior and then use excursions.mc <http://excursions.mc>, it would be like using excursions.inla without the VB corrections.

An easy way to test this would be to run your code with the VB corrections turned off, and then check if the results match more closely.

If this indeed is the case, then you should get more reliable results by using excursion.inla directly.

Best,
David

messages.body_plain:
In that model, the amount (and direction) of anisotropy would be controlled by B, and the range in the direction orthogonal to B is determined by \kappa. The standard deviation will be decided by a combination of all three parameters (see Example 2 in the original nested SPDE paper).

Note that you would have precision matrix H^-1 Q0 H^{-T}, where Q0 and H are sparse. So if you implement it in rgeneric you would need to merge H with the A matrix to get a sparse approximation. In this case, you need to assume that the parameters of H are fixed, since the A matrix is not allowed to depend on parameters in R-INLA.

There is some (very old) code for defining and sampling models like this based on R-INLA functions here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1T3nK8D7wengCT_A9jVIbZGSoVm9R4UDz/view

messages.body_plain:
The reason for setting b0 = 1 is just a parameterization choice so that we can keep the usual parameter \tau in the model without getting an over-parametrized model: So the model that is used there is (\kappa^2 - \Delta) (\tau u) = (1 + v^T\nabla)W, which can be reformulated as (\kappa^2 - \Delta) u = (b + B^T\nabla)W for b = 1/\tau and B = v/\tau.

Regarding the second question, since the model is not Markov, the trick is to realize that you can write X ~ N(0, (H^-1 Q0 H^{-T})^{-1}) as X =  H w0, where w0 ~ N(0,Q0^{-1}), so w0 is the latent GMRF that would be used in INLA. Then if you have the likelihood Y = AX + e for example, this is Y= AHw0 + e, so that AH would be the "observation matrix" for the latent  field w0.

-David

However, the right thing should be that if I use the rgeneric function in INLA, the Q matrix is still Q0 and the observation matrix should be AH where A is constructed by inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc) because here we treat A and H as fixed. And if we want to use INLA, that is we still hold the Markov property, we can only use w0 instead of X=Hw0. Please let me know if I made any mistakes.

Yours,
Yimeng Wang

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Quick question. Or in other words, I do not need rgeneric function because I only need to change the observation matrix and do not need to change the precision matrix. Can I simply use AH = A %*% H as observation matrix to construct the stack?

Yours,
Yimeng

> Hi David,
>
> Here is my understanding. In my previous code, I used the rgeneric function and defined the Q=H^-1 Q0 H^{-T} but did not change A. However, the right thing should be that if I use the rgeneric function in INLA, the Q matrix is still Q0 and the observation matrix should be AH where A is constructed by inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc) because here we treat A and H as fixed. And if we want to use INLA, that is we still hold the Markov property, we can only use w0 instead of X=Hw0. Please let me know if I made any mistakes.
>
> Yours,
> Yimeng Wang
>

> > On Wed, Apr 5, 2023 at 12:09 PM David Bolin <da...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> > > The reason for setting b0 = 1 is just a parameterization choice so that we can keep the usual parameter \tau in the model without getting an over-parametrized model: So the model that is used there is (\kappa^2 - \Delta) (\tau u) = (1 + v^T\nabla)W, which can be reformulated as (\kappa^2 - \Delta) u = (b + B^T\nabla)W for b = 1/\tau and B = v/\tau.
> > >
> > > Regarding the second question, since the model is not Markov, the trick is to realize that you can write X ~ N(0, (H^-1 Q0 H^{-T})^{-1}) as X =  H w0, where w0 ~ N(0,Q0^{-1}), so w0 is the latent GMRF that would be used in INLA. Then if you have the likelihood Y = AX + e for example, this is Y= AHw0 + e, so that AH would be the "observation matrix" for the latent  field w0.
> > >
> > > -David

Yes, that is correct. Unless you merge A and H, you need to use the dense matrix Q=H^-1 Q0 H^{-T} as precision, which will be very slow. If you treat H as fixed, then you should indeed be able to just use A %*% H in the stack for the standard spde model.

-David

> David

messages.subject: Recommended sampling method
messages.body_plain:
INLA has various functions for sampling marginals of hyperparameters, which is the recommended one when they give different results (beyond just differences due to sampling)?

In my case, for example, for the variance of a random effect,

1 / INLA::inla.hyperpar.sample(1e4, model, improve.marginals = T)[, 4]

and

INLA::inla.rmarginal(1e4, INLA::inla.tmarginal(fun = function(x) 1 / x, model$marginals.hyperpar[[4]]))

givea a notably wider distribution than

INLA::inla.posterior.sample.eval(
                       samples = INLA::inla.posterior.sample(1e4, model),
                       fun = function(...) {
                         1 / theta[4]
                       })

which in turn is much wider than

apply(sapply(model$marginals.random[[3]], # 3 is correct
             function(marg) INLA::inla.rmarginal(1e4, marg)),
      1,
      var)

Using int.strategy = "grid" is not computationally feasible in my case.

Best,
William L. Wetzel

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit quality
messages.body_plain:
Presumably you’re using an observation model with a log-link, such as Poisson?
Then your constructed covariate is very badly adapted, since it’s linear in the response instead of the log.  (And on log-scale, standard deviation 10 is extremely large, so the added noise doesn’t help). I’m guessing the estimated coefficient came out as small as well.

Finn

I meant that you would have to look at the component estimates to perhaps figure out what the problem is. Such as precisely checking whether the coefficient estimate you expected to be close to 1 was indeed close to 1. Now yup that you confirmed that you can continue further until you identify the part of the model that doesn’t behave as you expected. (And also check the obvious; the predictor estimate is only the estimate of the location parameter of the model, and you need to have set link=1 in he appropriate place, etc, etc)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Recommended sampling method
messages.body_plain:
A inla.hyperpar.sample()  sample from the hyperparameters, from their
joint approximations

B from this join distribution, the marginals are computed (by an
approximate method), which you can sample with 'inla.rmarginal'

C inla.posterior.sample() (and the use of inla.posterior.sample.eval()),
sample from the joint (hyperparam, latent), BUT for comptuational
issues, uses the integration points only for the hyperparameters, hence
treat them as discrete.

if you're interested in a function of the hyperparameters only, use A, a
function of the latent (with optional hyperparameters) use C.

On Fri, 2023-04-07 at 05:45 -0700, William L. Wetzel wrote:
> INLA has various functions for sampling marginals of hyperparameters,
> which is the recommended one when they give different results (beyond
> just differences due to sampling)?
>
> In my case, for example, for the variance of a random effect,
>
> 1 / INLA::inla.hyperpar.sample(1e4, model, improve.marginals = T)[, 4]
>
> and
>
> INLA::inla.rmarginal(1e4, INLA::inla.tmarginal(fun = function(x) 1 /
> x, model$marginals.hyperpar[[4]]))
>
> givea a notably wider distribution than
>
> INLA::inla.posterior.sample.eval(
>                        samples = INLA::inla.posterior.sample(1e4,
> model),
>                        fun = function(...) {
>                          1 / theta[4]
>                        })
>
> which in turn is much wider than
>
> apply(sapply(model$marginals.random[[3]], # 3 is correct
>              function(marg) INLA::inla.rmarginal(1e4, marg)),
>       1,
>       var)
>
> Using int.strategy = "grid" is not computationally feasible in my
> case.
>
> Best,
> William L. Wetzel

messages.body_plain:
Hi all，
I am new to INLA.
In a word:
I encountered trouble when using "copy". I wonder if there is a way to control the contribution of both models to the final space effect.
In details,
I used  prevalence data(point-referenced)to build spde model. And , I used incidence data (area data, provincial level ) to build the spde mode in the same region to provide some spatial information. Due to  point-referenced data are insufficient to build to a steady spde model.  However,  area data  contributes almost 2/3  random effect in the final result. I would like to know if is there a method to control the degree of impact of area data. (For example, I want to have 10% of the contribution form area data and 90% from point data in the results of spatial effects.)

Here is my formula:

gaus.prior <- list(prior="gaussian", param = c(1,2))

for1 <- c("-1","Intercept","f(field,model=spde,hyper=hyper)","f(loc_id,model='iid')")

### field represents modeling point data

for2 <- c("b0","f(field_inc ,copy='field',fixed=T ,hyper=list(theta=gaus.prior))")

### field_inc represents modeling area data

formula <- as.formula(paste(“y" ~ ，paste(paste(for1, collapse="+"), paste(paste(for2, collapse="+"), sep="+")))

result <- inla(formula,
               data=inla.stack.data(stack.full,spde=spde),
               family=c("binomial","poisson"),
               Ntrials=inla.stack.data(stack.full)$Ntrials,
               E=inla.stack.data(stack.full)$E,
               control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE,
                                      A=inla.stack.A(stack.full),
                                      quantiles=c(0.025,0.5,0.975),
                                      link=link),
               control.compute = list(dic=TRUE,config=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),
               control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),
               verbose=T)

the best option is to do the parameterisation and the priors, so that
you can actually specify this in the model. this is what's behind

and the relevant publication

Fuglstad, Geir-Arne, Ingeborg Gullikstad Hem, Alexander Knight, Håvard
Rue, and Andrea Riebler. 2020. “Intuitive Joint Priors for Variance
Parameters.” Bayesian Anal. 15 (4): 1109–37.

please check this out if this what you need.

Also the model

	inla.doc("bym2")

is an example of a similar construction.

Best
H

s <- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(r)

plot(cpo,  s$cv, log = "xy", pty = 19)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] LGCP cross validation question
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
cross validation for LGCPs is non-trivial, as the observations ar
"space and points", instead of "value at a point". THat means that for
example "leave-one-out cross-validation" is not a well defined
concept. People (including in Glasgow...) are working on
semi-automated alternatives for point processes, but there isn't a
pre-made code interface for that at this time.  One _can_ reformulate
the estimation and posterior predictions manually, to leave out
portions of space and predict the posterior point count in the left
out region, but it's a bit tricky to write the code for that (and it's
also slow).
For inlabru, there's a vignette about point process _residuals_, which
isn't cross validation, but that can provide similar insights for
model comparisons, in particular regarding how well each model
captures the spatial variability at different spatial scales.
See https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/2d_lgcp_residuals.html
which was developed as an Edinburgh student research project last
year.
(The online version will get updated within the next 30 minutes or so
to use terra instead of raster, and to make more internal use of sf)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] prediction with state-space model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for the basic version of this type of prediction you need to include
the prediction months in the original model, so yes, you need to add
group 13 as part of the model itself.
You can do this by specifying 13 months to inla.spde.make.index(), and
you also need to specify this when calling inla.spde.make.A() to make
it setup the correct "group model" structure.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

To figure out what’s happening, you may need to be more systematic. For example, you mentioned the quantity “ numCasos/offset(log(population))”, which clearly makes no sense; numCasos/population is probably the quantity you were thinking of.

I’m guessing the -12 intercept estimate is compensating for the average log-population offset in your model. The model is forced to use the log-population as an offset even when you include the near-perfect covariate, which explains why the covariate estimate doesn’t come out even closer to 1 than you got; it’s not perfect in the presence of the log-population offset.

Personally, I would prefer placing the population information in the E-parameter instead of as a fixed formula offset, so that the “fitted values” would be a per-individual parameter. Although for the testing, it would have the same effect on the model estimate as when used as offset.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Your “option 3” results are exactly as one should expect; coefficient estimate near 1, and the other covariate estimate near zero, and intercept near zero.

The E parameter means precisely this in the pure possion observations context:
When the observed value is Y, the linear predictor is eta, then
Y ~ Poisson( E * exp(eta) )
The E parameter is called “exposure” in some contexts, and in others it’s “population under risk” (when exp(eta) is a small hazard probability).

If it’s linked to just space or to space-time depends entirely on your model construction; each E value is attached to one observation.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit quality 2
messages.body_plain:
How to compute E needs a demography/epidemiological knowledge and accounts for what the model is being fitted for. Usually, E depends on gender and age specific marginal rates in order to model standardized rates. If you assume that the population in each area has similar age and gender structure, then you can use the raw overall rate times the population at risk for each time period. If you use a rate for each year, you are then including temporal variation (without modeling it).

messages.subject_clean: Exponential survival: low estimates and narrow intervals
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I found weird results when I fit an exponential survival model. I simulated some data for survival analysis and fitted a model with two fixed effects using three different families: coxph, exponential.surv, and weibull.surv. Models with coxph and weibull gave similar fixed effect estimates while the exponential model gave some estimates that are really close to the intercept value with narrow intervals. I tried different seeds but I always found these narrow results by the exponential model. Is there any explanation for these results? Attached is the code I used to generate the results.

Thank you.

Kind regards,
Yessika

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fit quality 2
messages.body_plain:
Hi Moisés,

I am not sure if I properly understood your concern. Assuming that you have an exposure, making a "perfect" covariate does not make things to match once you include both in the model.

About the absolute measures, let me try to illustrate with an example why abs measures are not ideal for when the link function is not identity.

n <- 30
x <- rnorm(n)
E <- rgamma(n, 10, 1e-5)

y <- rpois(n, E * exp(-7 + x))
summary(y)

result <- glm(y ~ x, poisson, offset = log(E))

fitt <- fitted(result)
fit.err <- fitt - y

plot(y ~ fitt)
abline(c(0, 1))

c(mae = mean(abs(fit.err)),
  mse = mean(fit.err^2))

## however:
summary(y/fitt)

## explore the "assintotia" for the residual deviance
x0 <- seq(0.1, 2*n, 0.1)
plot(x0, dchisq(x0, n-2), type = "l")
abline(v = deviance(result), col = 2, lwd = 4)

Best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Is it possible to construct a Geostatistical INLA Model with Decaying Buffer Zones?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to construct a Geostatistical INLA Model with Decaying Buffer Zones?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a geostatistical binomial model, running with the inla code below (You will find attached all required data for model recreation).

Each geostatistical point contains as data the number of individuals positive for a disease (Data$Count) and the number of individuals that were tested (Data$Total).

I was wondering whether it is possible in inla to incorporate a buffer zone (radius) around each geostatistical point that essentially represents the range of locations from which tested individuals were recruited from (Data$Range). Keep in mind that each buffer zone will be unique to each geostatistical point and should ideally be defined using a distance decay function to model the intensity decrease when approaching the end of each buffer zone.

Is this possible? If so could someone guide/advice me on how to achieve this?

Model code:
# Load Data
China <- st_read("China.shp")
Raster <- raster('Raster.tif')
Data <- read_excel("Data.xlsx")
Data <- st_as_sf(Data, coords = c("Lon", "Lat"), crs = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")

# Non-sampled coordinates
Unsampled <- rasterToPoints(Raster, spatial = TRUE)
Unsampled <- data.matrix(data.frame(lon = Unsampled$x, lat = Unsampled$y))

# Sampled coordinates
Sampled <- data.matrix(data.frame(lon = as.numeric((format(round(do.call(rbind, st_geometry(Data$geometry)), 5), nsmall = 5))[,2]),
                                  lat = as.numeric((format(round(do.call(rbind, st_geometry(Data$geometry)), 5), nsmall = 5))[,1])))

# Mesh construction
Boundary <-  as(China$geometry[[1]], "Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
Mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = Boundary, loc = Sampled, crs = crs,
                     max.edge = c(1,2)*diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/(3*5),
                     offset = c(diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/(3*5), diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/3),
                     cutoff = (diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/(3*5))/5)

# Projector Matrices
A_Sampled <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh, loc = Sampled)
A_Unsampled <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh, loc = Unsampled)

# SPDE
SPDE <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = Mesh, alpha = 1, constr = TRUE)

# Spatial Effect Index
S_Index  <- inla.spde.make.index(name ="s", n.spde = SPDE$n.spde)

# Stack
Stack_Sampled <- inla.stack(tag = "point",
                            data = list(y = Data$Count, Sample = Data$Total),
                            A = list(1, A_Sampled),
                            effects = list(Intercept = rep(1, nrow(Sampled)), s = S_Index))

Stack_Unsampled <- inla.stack(tag = "pred",
                              data = list(y = NA, Sample = NA),
                              A = list(1, A_Unsampled),
                              effects = list(data.frame(Intercept = rep(1, nrow(Unsampled))), s = S_Index))

Stack <- inla.stack(Stack_Sampled, Stack_Unsampled)

# Model
Formula <- y ~ 0 + Intercept + f(s, model = SPDE)

Model <- inla(Formula,
                    family = "binomial",
                    Ntrials = Sample,
                    data = inla.stack.data(Stack),
                    control.family = list(link = "logit"),
                    control.inla = list(int.strategy = "auto"),
                    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, A = inla.stack.A(Stack), link = 1),
                    control.compute = list(config = TRUE, dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE))

> I have a geostatistical binomial model, running with the inla code
> below (You will find attached all required data for model recreation).
>
> Each geostatistical point contains as data the number of individuals
> positive for a disease (Data$Count) and the number of individuals that
> were tested (Data$Total).
>
> I was wondering whether it is possible in inla to incorporate a buffer
> zone (radius) around each geostatistical point that essentially
> represents the range of locations from which tested individuals were
> recruited from (Data$Range). Keep in mind that each buffer zone will
> be unique to each geostatistical point and should ideally be defined
> using a distance decay function to model the intensity decrease when
> approaching the end of each buffer zone.
>
> Is this possible? If so could someone guide/advice me on how to
> achieve this?
>
> Model code:
> # Load Data
> China <- st_read("China.shp")
> Raster <- raster('Raster.tif')
> Data <- read_excel("Data.xlsx")
> Data <- st_as_sf(Data, coords = c("Lon", "Lat"), crs = "+proj=longlat
> +datum=WGS84")
>
> # Non-sampled coordinates
> Unsampled <- rasterToPoints(Raster, spatial = TRUE)
> Unsampled <- data.matrix(data.frame(lon = Unsampled$x, lat =
> Unsampled$y))
>
> # Sampled coordinates
> Sampled <- data.matrix(data.frame(lon =
> as.numeric((format(round(do.call(rbind, st_geometry(Data$geometry)),
> 5), nsmall = 5))[,2]),
>                                   lat =
> as.numeric((format(round(do.call(rbind, st_geometry(Data$geometry)),
> 5), nsmall = 5))[,1])))
>
> # Mesh construction
> Boundary <-  as(China$geometry[[1]], "Spatial") %>% inla.sp2segment()
> Mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = Boundary, loc = Sampled, crs = crs,
>                      max.edge = c(1,2)*diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/(3*5),
>                      offset = c(diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/(3*5),
> diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/3),
>                      cutoff = (diff(range(Sampled[,1]))/(3*5))/5)
>
> # Projector Matrices
> A_Sampled <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh, loc = Sampled)
> A_Unsampled <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh, loc = Unsampled)
>
> # SPDE
> SPDE <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = Mesh, alpha = 1, constr = TRUE)
>
> # Spatial Effect Index

>
> # Stack
> Stack_Sampled <- inla.stack(tag = "point",
>                             data = list(y = Data$Count, Sample =
> Data$Total),
>                             A = list(1, A_Sampled),

> nrow(Sampled)), s = S_Index))
>

>                               A = list(1, A_Unsampled),
>                               effects = list(data.frame(Intercept =
> rep(1, nrow(Unsampled))), s = S_Index))
>
> Stack <- inla.stack(Stack_Sampled, Stack_Unsampled)
>
> # Model
> Formula <- y ~ 0 + Intercept + f(s, model = SPDE)
>
> Model <- inla(Formula,
>                     family = "binomial",
>                     Ntrials = Sample,
>                     data = inla.stack.data(Stack),
>                     control.family = list(link = "logit"),
>                     control.inla = list(int.strategy = "auto"),
>                     control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, A =

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] elevation at mesh vertices
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

To aggregate gridded elevation onto the mesh I would suggest doing

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = grid_locations)
values_on_mesh <- (t(A) %*% grid_values) / colSums(A)

This takes the weighted averages of elevation, with weights equal to
the "hat" basis functions on the mesh.
(Your alternative formula with "/ A^T" isn't well defined since A is a
matrix, and you need to use the A matrix for the gridded locations.)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] elevation at mesh vertices
messages.body_plain:
That just means you don't have elevation information everywhere.
Hopefully it's in the outer border and doesn't directly connect to
your actual observation model. In that case, you can fill in the
missing values e.g. with the help of inlabru::bru_fill_missing() :

dat <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(mesh$loc[is.finite(values_on_mesh), ,
drop = FALSE], data = data.frame(values =
values_on_mesh[is.finite(values_on_mesh)]))
values_on_mesh <- inlabru::bru_fill_missing(
  data = dat,
  where = mesh$loc,
  values_on_mesh,
  layer = "values"
)

If the problem is instead that your elevation isn't available on a
dense enough grid, then you could still try the above, but finding a
denser topography data set (ETOPO at some resolution e.g.) might be
better.

Before using the aggregated/expanded covariate, take a look at it with
library(inlabru)
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() + gg(mesh, color = values_on_mesh)

If you do that with the version with NaN in it, you might see where
the problem is with those.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is it possible to construct a Geostatistical INLA Model with Decaying Buffer Zones?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Is it possible to construct a Geostatistical INLA Model with Decaying Buffer Zones?
messages.body_plain:
I suppose the purpose would be to modify it into aggregated observations but i wouldn't want to modify it into an areal data analysis as a lot of the predictive resolution would be lost.

Example for context:
Each geostatistical point represents the prevalence data of different studies.
A study was conducted for 100 individuals in cities A and B.
50 individuals were positive for the disease so the prevalence is 50%  (50 positive counts/ 100 tested individuals * 100).
The coordinates for this study are determine as the centroid coordinates between cities A and B.
This centoid will act as the 'hot spot' with prevalence 50%.
Lets assume that the furthest coordinate where individuals were recruited from within cities A and B for this study was 10km from the centroid.
So the buffer zone will be a circle with 10km radius from the centroid.
The prevalence should remain as 50% in the whole of the buffer zone but the weight of this value should gradually decrease when approaching the end of the buffer zone.
This is repeated for each study.
The resulting  buffer zones will vary in size and potentially overlap.

Please let me know if anything is unclear.

messages.subject: New stable version 23.04.24
messages.body_plain:
There is a new stable version out:  23.04.24

Apart for usual developments, which is available by

	 news(package="INLA")

there is also a recent fix for a inconsistent treatment of offset() in
formula, and the the 'offset=' argument, and if it was part of the
linear predictor/fitted.values or not (since the stable version
22.12.16). The offsets inpact on the reported
linear.predictor/fitted.values for inla.mode="compact" (or
"experimental") and inla.mode="classic", was different, and that was not
intentional. The recent fix make the current  behaviour equal to the
classic one, so both the offsets are part of the linear predictor and
fitted values. Sorry for any inconvenience.

So the results are now like this

> r=inla(y ~ 1 + offset(off), data=data.frame(y=1, off=10))
> r$summary.fixed[,"mean"]
[1] -9
> r$summary.linear.predictor$mean
[1] 0.999983509
> r$summary.fitted.values$mean
[1] 0.9999918944
> r=inla(y ~ 1, offset=off, data=data.frame(y=1, off=10))
> r$summary.fixed[,"mean"]
[1] -9
> r$summary.linear.predictor$mean
[1] 0.999983509
> r$summary.fitted.values$mean
[1] 0.9999918944

Best wishes
Havard

--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial data type for constructing mesh
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial data type for constructing mesh
messages.body_plain:
The boundary inputs currently have to be inla.mesh.segment, but the
inlabru package has updated conversion functions from both sp and sf.
Just call inlabru::fm_as_inla_mesh_segment() (install from github or
r-universe to get the latest updated versions) on your polygons to
convert them to inla.mesh.segment objects.

The development of updated sf support is done within inlabru, but will
soon be separated out into a new fmesher package.

Finn
